title: Hatikvah

cards: A valley full of bones, very dry. That's the scene the prophet Ezekiel describes. In his vision, God tells him the bones are the whole house of Israel, and tells him what the people are saying, a sentence of despair.
Our bones are dried up, they say, and "our hope is lost". In Hebrew: avdah tikvatenu. Keep that phrase in your ear.
Long after Ezekiel, a poem answered it almost word for word. The poem became a song, the song became a national anthem, and its name, a single Hebrew word, is today's word.

teach.b: Hatikvah. Ha means the, and tikvah means hope: the hope. It's Israel's national anthem, and it's often sung at Jewish gatherings in other countries too.

teach.h: A SOUL YEARNS, AN EYE LOOKS TO ZION.
teach.b: In plain English, roughly: as long as, deep in the heart, a Jewish soul still yearns, and an eye still looks forward to the east, toward Zion, our hope is not yet lost, the hope of two thousand years: to be a free people in our land, the land of Zion and Jerusalem.

teach.h: OUR HOPE IS NOT YET LOST.
teach.b: The people said avdah tikvatenu, our hope is lost. The anthem sings od lo avdah tikvatenu, our hope is not yet lost. Two small words, od lo, not yet, turn despair around.
Before those words are even quoted, the bones have come together and breath has entered them, and right after, God promises to open the graves and bring the people home to the land of Israel.
Notice what kind of hope the anthem sings.

teach.h: A HOPE STILL HELD, NOT A VICTORY SONG.
teach.b: Not a victory song about something already won, but a hope still held, with the heart and the eyes, facing a direction.
The year met this kind of hope before: in prayers that faced Jerusalem, in exile after exile, in people who kept saying next year. People hear the anthem differently, too.
Israel has citizens who aren't Jewish, and some have said a song about a Jewish soul doesn't speak for them; that conversation is part of Israel's life.
But the word at the song's center is one the Bible and the anthem share.

how: Hatikvah is sung at state ceremonies in Israel and at Jewish community events, school graduations and gatherings in other countries, often with the audience standing.

o: the vision of Ezekiel's valley of dry bones
the return: a song for coming home to Zion
the hope: Israel's anthem, a hope not yet lost

s: ha means the, and tikvah means hope.
the anthem celebrates a victory already won
it sings of a hope not yet lost, still held, facing toward Zion.
the words our hope is lost come from the Bible
in Ezekiel 37:11, God reports that the house of Israel is saying them. the anthem answers: not yet lost.

games.q: you're writing words to answer Ezekiel's dry bones, who say our hope is lost. which two words do you put in front of their sentence?
games.why: od lo, not yet. the anthem sings od lo avdah tikvatenu: our hope is not yet lost.

practice: Find one hope you've carried for a while: not a wish for a thing, but a hope for a person, a place, a change that hasn't come yet, said in a few plain words. Then put the anthem's two small words in front of it: not yet.
If you pray, bring that hope before God in your own words; if you don't, simply keep it company, still unfinished, still held.

wordCard.voice: Hatikvah. The hope: Israel's anthem, which answers the dry bones' our hope is lost with our hope is not yet lost. Today's word.
